name: IIWF World Heavyweight Championship
epitaph: The federation's own top prize, crowned in a 24-man tournament at the fed's own first pay-per-view and carried, across eight recoverable reigns, into a title still live at the end of this collection's own 1998 holdings.
notes: Reconstructed from the fed's own weekly rankings-table markers and ring-announcer receipts; two changes (mid-1996, the vacancy-tournament result of July 1997) are dated only to a bounded window.

name: IIWF Intercontinental Championship
epitaph: Created by battle royal one week after the promotion's own first pay-per-view, this belt changed hands at least nine times across 1996 and 1997 with two of its later changes recorded only as bare announcement lines.
notes: Two 1997 changes (18 August, 24 September) survive only as announcement lines inside show bodies this pass did not read in full; the winners' names are not recovered here.

name: IIWF Cruiserweight Championship
epitaph: The promotion's own weight-class belt, changing hands across nine recoverable reigns through 1996 and 1997 with one late-1997 forfeiture line left unresolved by the fed's own surviving record.
notes: A forfeiture line to Richard "Moxy" Blue (29 November 1997) stands beside a Derek Mota reclamation the same December; the collection's own holdings do not resolve which is the title's own last word for the year.

name: IIWF World Tag Team Championship
epitaph: Crowned in a ten-team, two-ring clash at the promotion's own first pay-per-view, this title's lineage runs clean through early 1997 and tangles across August to November, where this collection's own holdings carry two teams both claiming it at once.
notes: The August-November 1997 stretch (a Midsummer Madness change to the Syndicate, a Golden Grapple lyric crediting Cold Spell) is the messiest run in the fed's own record and is registered here as partially unresolved rather than silently picking one line.

name: IIWF United States Tag Team Championship
epitaph: Created on air in February 1997 because the fed's own Executive Committee judged its rivals were winning the tag-team wars, crowned at that spring's Ring Wars III, and billed as defunct by that same November — a complete founding-to-abolition arc inside a single year.
notes: The fed's own Golden Grapple Awards stage direction (22 November 1997) calls the belt "defunct" as a prop description; no formal retirement announcement survives in this collection's holdings.
